observation_summary: The JsonParserSequence skips a token when switching between concatenated parsers, causing the parser to return the wrong value (3 instead of 2) in the test case.
hypothesis: The root cause is an incorrect procedural step in the nextToken() implementation of JsonParserSequence. When switching to a new delegate parser, the code calls nextToken() on the new parser prematurely, effectively skipping the first token of the second parser.
prediction: The fix will involve modifying the nextToken() method in JsonParserSequence to check if the new delegate parser is already positioned at a valid token before calling nextToken() on it, or otherwise adjusting the state transition logic to avoid the redundant call.
experiment_rationale: The bug report explicitly states that nextToken() calls nextToken() on the new delegate, causing a token to be missed. This is a procedural logic error in how the sequence manages its delegate parsers.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a procedural error in the sequence management logic. It is not a missing guard (Checking), not a wrong constant (Assignment), and not a design-level capability omission (Function/Class/Object). It is a flaw in the algorithm used to iterate through tokens across multiple parsers.
evidence_used: Bug report description: 'JsonParserSequence's nextToken() calls nextToken() on the new delegate which may cause that we miss a token.'

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While a check might be added to fix it, the core issue is the procedural logic of the sequence iteration, not just a missing validation.
The issue is internal to the JsonParserSequence implementation, not a mismatch in the contract between the sequence and the delegate parsers.
